questions.text: Explain tokenization in NLP and why it is important.
questions.reference_answer: Tokenization is the process of splitting raw text into smaller units called tokens, such as words, subwords or characters. It is usually the first step of an NLP pipeline, and later steps such as stop-word removal, stemming, POS tagging and vectorisation all operate on tokens. A good tokenizer must handle punctuation, contractions and other special cases correctly.

answers.text: Tokenisation means breaking a piece of text into small meaningful pieces, usually words but sometimes sub-words or single characters. Because almost every later stage of an NLP system - stemming, tagging, building vectors - works on these pieces, it is normally done first. questions.text: What is TF-IDF? Explain how it assigns weights to terms.
questions.reference_answer: TF-IDF (term frequency - inverse document frequency) is a statistic that weights how important a word is to a document in a collection. Term frequency counts how often the term appears in the document. Inverse document frequency measures how rare the term is across the corpus and is computed as log(N / df), where N is the number of documents and df is the number of documents containing the term. The TF-IDF weight is the product TF x IDF. Words that occur in almost every document, such as 'the', get a weight close to zero, while words that are distinctive for a document get a high weight.

rubric.description: Term frequency counts how often a term occurs in a document

rubric.label: Inverse document frequency
rubric.description: Inverse document frequency measures how rare a term is across the corpus, computed as log(N / df) where N is the number of documents and df the number of documents containing the term

rubric.label: Weight = TF x IDF
rubric.description: The TF-IDF weight of a term is the product of its TF and IDF values

rubric.label: Effect on common vs distinctive words
rubric.description: Words common to many documents such as 'the' get a low weight while distinctive words get a high weight

answers.text: TF-IDF is a way of scoring words in a document. The first part, term frequency, is simply how many times the word appears in that document. The second part, IDF, is the log of the total number of documents divided by the number of documents that contain the word, so rare words get a big value. Multiplying the two gives the final score. As a result, words like 'is' or 'the' that appear everywhere end up with almost zero weight, while words that are specific to a document stand out.

questions.reference_answer: Stemming removes suffixes from words using simple heuristic rules, for example with the Porter stemmer, so the resulting stem may not be a real word (studies becomes studi). Lemmatization uses a vocabulary and morphological analysis, often together with the part of speech, to return the dictionary form of a word, called the lemma (better becomes good). Lemmatization is therefore more accurate but slower than stemming.

questions.text: What are word embeddings? How do they differ from one-hot encoding?
questions.reference_answer: One-hot encoding represents each word as a sparse vector whose length equals the vocabulary size, with a single 1 and all other values 0. Such vectors are orthogonal, so they carry no notion of similarity between words. Word embeddings are dense, low-dimensional, real-valued vectors. They are learned from the contexts in which words appear (the distributional hypothesis), for example with Word2Vec or GloVe. As a result, words with similar meanings get nearby vectors and embeddings capture semantic relationships such as king - man + woman = queen.

rubric.label: One-hot has no similarity

answers.text: With one-hot encoding every word gets a vector whose length equals the vocabulary size, filled with zeros except a single one, so the vectors are huge and sparse. Since any two such vectors are orthogonal, the encoding cannot tell that 'cat' is closer to 'dog' than to 'car'. Word embeddings fix this by giving each word a short, dense vector of real numbers, for example 300 dimensions. These vectors are trained from the words that surround each word in a large corpus, as in Word2Vec or GloVe. As a result, related words end up close together and even analogies like king - man + woman = queen work.

questions.text: Explain Named Entity Recognition (NER) and its applications.
questions.reference_answer: Named Entity Recognition locates named entities in unstructured text and classifies them into predefined categories. Typical categories are person, organization, location, date and money. It is used for information extraction, in search engines, question answering systems and chatbots. NER is usually solved as a sequence labelling task with BIO tags, using CRFs or deep learning models such as BiLSTM-CRF or BERT.

questions.text: What are stop words? When should stop-word removal be avoided?
questions.reference_answer: Stop words are very frequent function words such as 'the', 'is' and 'and' that carry little meaning on their own. Removing them reduces noise and the size of the data, which makes tasks such as search and text classification more efficient. However, they should not be removed when they carry meaning, for example negations like 'not' in sentiment analysis, or in machine translation and exact phrase search.

questions.text: How does a database index improve query performance? Mention its drawbacks.
questions.reference_answer: An index is a separate data structure, typically a B-tree or a hash table, that maps column values to the locations of the rows containing them. It lets the database find matching rows without scanning the whole table, so lookups take logarithmic instead of linear time. Indexes cost extra storage and slow down inserts, updates and deletes because the index must be maintained. They should therefore be created on columns that are frequently used in WHERE clauses, joins or sorting.

answers.text: A database index works like the index at the back of a book: it is an extra structure, usually a B-tree, that stores the values of a column together with pointers to the rows that hold them. Instead of reading every row in the table, the engine walks the tree and jumps straight to the matching rows, so searching takes roughly log n steps. The price is additional disk space and slower writes, since every insert or update must also update the index. That is why we index only columns that appear often in WHERE conditions, joins or ORDER BY.

questions.text: Explain the bag-of-words model and its limitations.
questions.reference_answer: The bag-of-words model represents a document as a vector of word counts (or presence values) over a fixed vocabulary built from the corpus. It ignores grammar and word order, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' get the same vector. Because the vocabulary is large, the vectors are high-dimensional and sparse. It also cannot capture meaning or similarity between words: synonyms such as 'car' and 'automobile' are treated as unrelated features.

rubric.description: Bag of words represents a document as a vector of word counts or presence over a fixed vocabulary

rubric.description: The vectors are high-dimensional and sparse because the vocabulary is large

rubric.label: No semantic similarity
rubric.description: It cannot capture meaning or similarity between words, so synonyms are treated as unrelated

answers.text: In the bag-of-words approach we first build a vocabulary of all words in the corpus and then describe each document by how many times every vocabulary word occurs in it. The arrangement of the words is thrown away, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' get exactly the same vector. Because the vocabulary can contain tens of thousands of words, these vectors are very long and mostly zeros. Another weakness is that it has no idea of meaning: 'car' and 'automobile' are just two unrelated columns.

questions.text: What is overfitting in machine learning and how can it be prevented?
questions.reference_answer: Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data, including its noise, too closely instead of the general pattern. An overfitted model performs very well on the training data but poorly on unseen test data, meaning it generalises badly. It can be detected by comparing training and validation error, for example with cross-validation. It can be prevented with regularisation (L1/L2), more training data, early stopping, dropout or a simpler model.

answers.text: A model overfits when it memorises the examples it was trained on, noise and all, instead of learning the general pattern. You can see it when accuracy on the training set is excellent but accuracy on new data is much worse. Keeping a separate validation set, or using k-fold cross-validation, shows the gap between the two errors. To avoid it we can collect more data, add L1/L2 regularisation, use dropout, stop training early or choose a less complex model.

questions.text: State Newton's third law of motion and explain it with an example.
questions.reference_answer: Newton's third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction: when one body exerts a force on a second body, the second body exerts a force of equal magnitude in the opposite direction on the first. The action and reaction forces act on two different bodies, so they do not cancel each other. For example, a rocket pushes exhaust gases backwards and the gases push the rocket forwards; similarly a gun recoils when a bullet is fired.

questions.text: What is part-of-speech (POS) tagging? Why is it a challenging task?
questions.reference_answer: Part-of-speech tagging assigns a grammatical category such as noun, verb, adjective or adverb to each word in a sentence. It is challenging because many words are ambiguous and their correct tag depends on context; for example 'book' is a noun in 'read the book' but a verb in 'book a ticket'. Taggers therefore use statistical or neural sequence models such as HMMs with the Viterbi algorithm, CRFs or BiLSTMs trained on annotated corpora like the Penn Treebank. POS tags are used in downstream tasks such as parsing, named entity recognition, lemmatization and information extraction.

rubric.label: Downstream uses
rubric.description: POS tags are used in downstream tasks such as parsing, named entity recognition, lemmatization and information extraction

answers.text: POS tagging labels every word in a sentence with its word class - noun, verb, adjective, adverb and so on. The hard part is ambiguity: 'book' is a noun in 'read the book' but a verb in 'book a ticket', so the tagger must look at the neighbouring words. Modern taggers learn this from hand-annotated corpora such as the Penn Treebank using HMMs with the Viterbi algorithm, CRFs or neural networks. The tags are then fed to later steps like syntactic parsing, lemmatization and entity recognition.
POS tagging means marking each word as a noun, verb, adjective etc.
The same word can have different tags in different sentences, for example 'run' can be a noun or a verb, so context is needed.

POS = part of speech. Tagger assigns N/V/ADJ tags to each token. Ambiguity: 'book' (N vs V) resolved using context. Models: HMM + Viterbi, CRF, BiLSTM trained on tagged corpora. Used in parsing, NER, lemmatization.

Machine translation converts text from one language to another, for example English to Hindi. Early systems used hand-written rules and dictionaries. Later, statistical systems learned from parallel corpora of translated sentences. Today, neural networks with attention, such as the Transformer, give the best translation quality and are used by Google Translate.
